newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq oil in two days as Baghdad plans export rush.
newsitem.headline: Iraq oil in two days as Baghdad plans export rush.

text.p: Iraq said on Monday it would resume exporting oil within two days under the second phase of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
Baghdad said it would aim for a new post-Gulf War export record in a bid to raise as much cash as possible before an interim deadline in early September.

Oil Minister Amir Muhammed Rasheed, quoted by the official Iraqi news agency INA, said the first tanker had docked on Monday at the Turkish port of Ceyhan to be loaded with a two-million-barrel shipment.

"The supertanker Arcadia has docked today in the Turkish Ceyhan port in order to be loaded with two million barrels for the favour of a company....whose contract (with Iraq) is expected to be approved (by the United Nations) within two days," said Rasheed.
Oil traders said U.S. company Bayoil had title to the Arcadia cargo for the North American market, Iraq's first shipment since the end of May.

Companies then scheduled to load before the end of the month from Ceyhan include U.S. Coastal, French Total, Spain's Repsol, U.S. Chevron, Turkey's Tupras, Russia's Rosneft and Nafta and Italy's Agip .
Rasheed said Iraq planned to export 30 million barrels of crude by the end of August in liftings from Ceyhan and its Gulf port of Mina al-Bakr.

That means Baghdad plans to export some 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) over the rest of August, its highest level since Gulf War sanctions were imposed after Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Traders said several million barrels of crude held in storage at Ceyhan and Mina al-Bakr would help boost export capacity over the next few weeks.

Shipping sources said preliminary plans were for at least 875,000 bpd from Ceyhan and the remainder from Mina al-Bakr, more than double the 670,000 bpd sold under the first phase of the U.N. exchange.
The oil-for-food deal between Iraq and the United Nations started last December and was renewed for another six months on June 8.
The deal allows Iraq to sell $2.14 billion worth of oil, including pipeline fees, over six months in exchange for food and medicine.

Sales must be divided into two equal 90-day periods. After a two-month delay waiting for a revised aid distribution plan, Baghdad has just 25 days to try to reach its interim $1 billion target by September 5.

On Sunday the head of Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO), Saddam Zeban Hassan, said in press remarks that Baghdad had renewed contracts with oil companies from the first six months of the deal, except for British, Japanese and Dutch firms.
Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch/Shell, British Petroleum and Japan's Mitsubishi have all said Iraq had declined to renew contracts for political reasons
